# Factors, Strings, and Dates {#sec-types} ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.* [Phil Karlton]{.smallcaps}, *attributed* (c. 1996) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Sources Stat 545 Chapters 10--13 (Jenny Bryan, UBC); the `forcats`, `stringr`, and `lubridate` packages. ::: ## Prerequisites Answer the following questions to see if you can bypass this chapter. You can find the answers at the end of the chapter in @sec-quiz-answers-14. 1. Why has `stringsAsFactors = FALSE` been the default since R 4.0, and what problems did the old default cause? 2. What does `stringr::str_detect()` return, and how does it differ from `stringr::str_extract()`? 3. Given `c('2026-04-23', '04/23/2026', 'April 23, 2026')`, write one `lubridate`/`readr` pipeline that parses all three into `Date` objects. ## Learning objectives By the end of this chapter you should be able to: - Manage factors idiomatically with `forcats` (reorder, lump, relevel, drop, infreq). - Use `stringr` verbs confidently for detection, extraction, replacement, splitting, and interpolation. - Parse dates robustly with `lubridate`, including mixed formats and time zones. - Diagnose and fix the common 'character vs. factor vs. ordered factor' decision that causes modeling errors downstream. - Recognize locale, time-zone, and Excel-date pitfalls. ## Orientation Numeric columns misbehave loudly. A value that should be a number and is not will stop the analysis, and the fix follows within the minute. Text, categories, and dates are the opposite case, and that is why they merit a chapter of their own. A date parsed under the wrong convention is still a date. A factor with an unintended reference level still fits. A string with trailing whitespace still joins, to nothing. Each of these produces a result rather than an error. Unfortunately, the result is wrong in a way that no amount of staring at the output will reveal, because the output looks exactly as it should. We take up here the three packages that make these types tractable. Master them, and a large share of biomedical data cleaning becomes routine. More to the point, the failures that remain become the loud kind. The packages are: - **`forcats`** for factors (categorical variables with defined levels). - **`stringr`** for character operations. - **`lubridate`** for dates and times. All three are part of the tidyverse, with consistent naming and pipe-friendly interfaces. ## The statistician's contribution {#sec-types-human} The three packages are well documented and pleasant to use. The bugs they exist to prevent are not bugs of syntax. They are bugs of timing and assumption: **Factor or character?** A character vector is flexible: any value, any order, any new level later. A factor is constrained: a fixed set of levels, a defined order, attached metadata. For analysis, factors are correct: the model needs to know the reference level and the level set. For data cleaning and joining, characters are usually safer (no surprises when a new value arrives). Convert to factor late, near the modeling step. **Reference levels matter.** A logistic regression with factor `treatment` and reference 'high-dose' produces coefficients with a different interpretation from one with reference 'placebo'. The default (alphabetical) is rarely what you want. Set the reference deliberately, in writing, in the data-cleaning script. **Time zones are tricky.** A 'date' value '2026-04-23' without a time zone is fine for daily-resolution analyses. A 'time' value '2026-04-23 02:00:00' is ambiguous: which time zone? UTC? US/Pacific? The local time zone of the machine that recorded it? Time-zone errors propagate quietly through analyses; daylight- saving transitions cause spurious 1-hour gaps. **Excel dates.** When data come from Excel, dates may arrive as 5-digit serial numbers ('45405') rather than date strings. Parsing them as dates produces nonsense (year 124, depending on the epoch convention). The fix is `janitor::excel_numeric_to_date()` or careful import. Verify any column whose name suggests dates but whose values are numeric. These judgments are what distinguish a working data cleaning script from one that silently mishandles a common type. The factor-or-character decision is not a matter of taste. Nor is it a decision made once. It is a decision about *when* in the pipeline the conversion happens, and @fig-factor-timing gives the answer this chapter argues for. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-factor-timing %%| fig-alt: "Left-to-right chain. Read, clean and recode, and join %%| all stay in character type. A highlighted node marks where to %%| convert to factor, setting the reference level deliberately. %%| From there the chain branches to Model and to Plot, both %%| working in factor type." %%| fig-cap: "Where to convert. Character is the safe type through %%| reading, cleaning, and joining, because a new or misspelled %%| value is merely a new string rather than an invalid level. %%| Factor is the correct type at modeling and plotting, because %%| the model needs a fixed level set and a declared reference." flowchart LR R["Read
character"] --> C["Clean and recode
character"] C --> J["Join
character"] J --> X["Convert here
factor, reference level
set deliberately"] X --> M["Model
factor"] X --> P["Plot
factor, ordered
by fct_reorder"] ``` ## Factors with `forcats` The standard operations: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(forcats) library(dplyr) library(palmerpenguins) f <- factor(c("low", "high", "low", "medium", "high")) # levels in current order levels(f) #> [1] "high" "low" "medium" #> [1] "high" "low" "medium" # alphabetical by default; reorder by frequency fct_infreq(f) #> [1] low high low medium high #> Levels: high low medium # reorder by another variable penguins |> mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, body_mass_g, mean, .na_rm = TRUE)) #> # A tibble: 344 x 8 #> species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g #> #> 1 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181 3750 #> 2 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 17.4 186 3800 #> 3 Adelie Torgersen 40.3 18 195 3250 #> 4 Adelie Torgersen NA NA NA NA #> 5 Adelie Torgersen 36.7 19.3 193 3450 #> 6 Adelie Torgersen 39.3 20.6 190 3650 #> 7 Adelie Torgersen 38.9 17.8 181 3625 #> 8 Adelie Torgersen 39.2 19.6 195 4675 #> 9 Adelie Torgersen 34.1 18.1 193 3475 #> 10 Adelie Torgersen 42 20.2 190 4250 #> # i 334 more rows #> # i 2 more variables: sex , year # specify order explicitly fct_relevel(f, "low", "medium", "high") #> [1] low high low medium high #> Levels: low medium high # combine rare levels fct_lump_n(f, n = 2) # keep top 2; rest -> 'Other' #> [1] low high low Other high #> Levels: high low Other fct_lump_min(f, min = 5) # keep levels with >= 5 obs #> [1] Other Other Other Other Other #> Levels: Other # drop unused levels fct_drop(f) #> [1] low high low medium high #> Levels: high low medium # rename levels fct_recode(f, "L" = "low", "M" = "medium", "H" = "high") #> [1] L H L M H #> Levels: H L M ``` ::: When to convert character to factor: - Just before modeling: ensures the model knows the level set and the reference. - Just before plotting: enables `fct_reorder` for ordered axis labels. When to keep as character: - During data cleaning: avoids 'invalid factor level' surprises when a new value arrives. - For joining: factor matching can fail when levels differ between tables. ## Strings with `stringr` Pattern detection, extraction, replacement, and splitting: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(stringr) s <- c("ABC123", "ABC", "XYZ-789", NA) # detect: returns logical str_detect(s, "[0-9]") #> [1] TRUE FALSE TRUE NA #> [1] TRUE FALSE TRUE NA # extract: returns first match per input, or NA str_extract(s, "[0-9]+") #> [1] "123" NA "789" NA #> [1] "123" NA "789" NA # extract all matches per input (returns list) str_extract_all(s, "[0-9]+") #> [[1]] #> [1] "123" #> #> [[2]] #> character(0) #> #> [[3]] #> [1] "789" #> #> [[4]] #> [1] NA # replace str_replace(s, "[0-9]+", "***") #> [1] "ABC***" "ABC" "XYZ-***" NA # split str_split("a,b,c,d", ",", simplify = TRUE) #> [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] #> [1,] "a" "b" "c" "d" #> [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] #> [1,] "a" "b" "c" "d" # interpolate name <- "World" str_glue("Hello, {name}!") #> Hello, World! #> Hello, World! # case str_to_lower("ABC") # "abc" #> [1] "abc" str_to_upper("abc") # "ABC" #> [1] "ABC" str_to_title("hello world") # "Hello World" #> [1] "Hello World" # trim whitespace str_trim(" abc ") # "abc" #> [1] "abc" str_squish(" a b c ") # "a b c" #> [1] "a b c" ``` ::: The regex fundamentals you need: - `[abc]`: any of a, b, c. - `[a-z]`, `[A-Z]`, `[0-9]`: ranges. - `\\d`, `\\w`, `\\s`: digit, word char, whitespace. - `*`, `+`, `?`: zero-or-more, one-or-more, zero-or-one. - `{n}`, `{n,m}`: exactly n, between n and m. - `^`, `$`: start, end of string. - `()`: capture group; `(?:...)` non-capturing. - `|`: alternation. - `\\`: escape; in R strings this is `\\\\` for a literal backslash. For complex regex, build incrementally and test each step. ## Dates with `lubridate` Parsing: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(lubridate) # fixed format ymd("2026-04-23") #> [1] "2026-04-23" mdy("4/23/2026") #> [1] "2026-04-23" dmy("23 April 2026") #> [1] "2026-04-23" # mixed formats: try each parse_date_time(c("2026-04-23", "04/23/2026", "April 23, 2026"), orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "Bdy")) #> [1] "2026-04-23 UTC" "2026-04-23 UTC" "2026-04-23 UTC" #> [1] "2026-04-23" "2026-04-23" "2026-04-23" # date-time ymd_hms("2026-04-23 14:30:00") #> [1] "2026-04-23 14:30:00 UTC" ymd_hm("2026-04-23 14:30") #> [1] "2026-04-23 14:30:00 UTC" ``` ::: Components: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} d <- ymd("2026-04-23") year(d) # 2026 #> [1] 2026 month(d) # 4 #> [1] 4 day(d) # 23 #> [1] 23 wday(d) # 5 (1 = Sunday by default) #> [1] 5 wday(d, label = TRUE) # Thu #> [1] Thu #> Levels: Sun < Mon < Tue < Wed < Thu < Fri < Sat ``` ::: Arithmetic: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} d + days(7) # 2026-04-30 #> [1] "2026-04-30" d %m+% months(3) # 2026-07-23 (handles month length safely) #> [1] "2026-07-23" # differences ymd("2026-12-31") - ymd("2026-01-01") # Time difference of 364 days #> Time difference of 364 days as.numeric(ymd("2026-12-31") - ymd("2026-01-01"), units = "days") #> [1] 364 ``` ::: Time zones: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # parse as a specific time zone t <- ymd_hms("2026-04-23 14:30:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles") t #> [1] "2026-04-23 14:30:00 PDT" # convert with_tz(t, "UTC") # same instant, different zone #> [1] "2026-04-23 21:30:00 UTC" force_tz(t, "UTC") # same wall clock, different zone #> [1] "2026-04-23 14:30:00 UTC" ``` ::: `with_tz` changes the displayed zone without changing the instant; `force_tz` changes the instant by declaring the wall clock was always in the new zone. Confusing them is a common source of 1- to 24-hour errors. ## A runnable example: parsing a messy clinical field The three tools of this chapter earn their place on the free-text fields that clinical data are full of. To illustrate, consider a single column recording a dosing instruction as the site typed it, with the drug, the amount, and the start date all run together and formatted inconsistently. We use a regular expression to pull out the structured pieces, and `lubridate` to parse the dates, which arrive in three different formats. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} reticulate::py_require("pandas") library(tidyverse) dosing <- tibble( raw = c("Metformin 500mg started 2026-01-14", "Lisinopril 10 mg started 01/22/2026", "Atorvastatin 20mg started Feb 3 2026", "Aspirin 81 mg started 2026-02-19") ) parsed <- dosing |> mutate( drug = str_extract(raw, "^[A-Za-z]+"), dose = as.integer(str_extract(raw, "\\d+(?=\\s?mg)")), date_s = str_extract(raw, "(?<=started ).*$"), start = parse_date_time(date_s, orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "bdy")) |> as_date() ) |> select(drug, dose, start) parsed #> # A tibble: 4 x 3 #> drug dose start #> #> 1 Metformin 500 2026-01-14 #> 2 Lisinopril 10 2026-01-22 #> 3 Atorvastatin 20 2026-02-03 #> 4 Aspirin 81 2026-02-19 ``` ::: Three regular-expression constructs do the work. The anchor `^[A-Za-z]+` takes the leading word, the drug. The lookahead `\\d+(?=\\s?mg)` takes the digits that precede `mg` without capturing the `mg` itself. The lookbehind `(?<=started )` takes everything after the word `started`, which is the date in whatever format the site used. `parse_date_time` then tries each candidate format in turn. The result is a tidy three-column table drawn from a single messy string. ### The same parsing in Python `pandas` exposes the same operations through its `.str` accessor and `to_datetime`. The regular expressions are identical, because the regex dialect is shared. Only the surrounding idiom differs. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd dosing = r.dosing # the R tibble, via reticulate out = pd.DataFrame({ "drug": dosing["raw"].str.extract(r"^([A-Za-z]+)")[0], "dose": dosing["raw"].str.extract(r"(\d+)\s?mg")[0].astype(int), "start": pd.to_datetime( dosing["raw"].str.extract(r"started (.*)$")[0], format="mixed"), }) out #> drug dose start #> 0 Metformin 500 2026-01-14 #> 1 Lisinopril 10 2026-01-22 #> 2 Atorvastatin 20 2026-02-03 #> 3 Aspirin 81 2026-02-19 ``` ::: The `format="mixed"` argument is `pandas`' counterpart to supplying several `orders` to `parse_date_time`. It lets each value be parsed by whichever format fits. The lesson is that regex and date parsing are portable skills. The drug, dose, and date fall out the same way in either language, and a biostatistician who knows the constructs can work in whichever the project uses. ::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true} ## Check your understanding: factor reference level **Question.** You fit `glm(outcome ~ treatment, family = binomial)` where `treatment` is a factor with levels `"placebo"`, `"low"`, `"high"`. The default reference is alphabetical (`"high"`). The intercept estimates 18.2 and the `treatmentplacebo` coefficient is -3.1. What is the mean outcome under high-dose treatment? **Answer.** The intercept estimates the linear-predictor value at the reference level (`"high"`). The high-dose mean on the link scale is therefore 18.2 (or its inverse-link transform, depending on the family). The `treatmentplacebo` coefficient (-3.1) is the difference from high-dose, so the placebo mean on the link scale is 18.2 - 3.1 = 15.1. For clinical reporting, it is usually clearer to set the reference deliberately to `"placebo"`, so the intercept gives the placebo baseline and the treatment coefficients give the increments from baseline: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} treatment <- c("high", "placebo", "low", "high", "placebo") treatment <- factor(treatment, levels = c("placebo", "low", "high")) levels(treatment) # placebo is now the reference #> [1] "placebo" "low" "high" ``` ::: The default alphabetical ordering is, unfortunately, a frequent source of misreported effect direction. ::: ## Common pitfalls **Excel dates as serial numbers.** A date column from Excel may arrive as `45405` (= 2024-04-23 in Excel's 1900-epoch numbering). Parse with: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} janitor::excel_numeric_to_date(45405) #> [1] "2024-04-23" #> [1] "2024-04-23" ``` ::: Verify: any 'date' column whose values are 5-digit numbers should ring an alarm. **Mixed-locale month names.** `lubridate::dmy()` can read 'avril' (French April) only if the locale supports it. For multi-language data: ```r lct <- Sys.getlocale("LC_TIME") Sys.setlocale("LC_TIME", "fr_FR.UTF-8") dmy("23 avril 2026") Sys.setlocale("LC_TIME", lct) # restore ``` Or use explicit format strings. **Time-zone-naïve datetimes.** A datetime read without a time zone defaults to UTC (lubridate) or the system zone (base R). Be explicit; never assume. **Daylight-saving transitions.** Adding 24 hours and adding 1 day are not always the same: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ymd_hms("2026-03-09 01:00:00", tz = "US/Pacific") + days(1) #> [1] "2026-03-10 01:00:00 PDT" #> [1] "2026-03-10 01:00:00 PDT" ymd_hms("2026-03-09 01:00:00", tz = "US/Pacific") + hours(24) #> [1] "2026-03-10 01:00:00 PDT" #> [1] "2026-03-10 02:00:00 PDT" ``` ::: The first is a calendar day. The second is 24 wall-clock hours, which crosses a DST boundary. Use whichever notion of a day is appropriate for the analysis at hand. ## Common antipatterns **Hand-coded `ifelse` chains for date parsing**: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c("04/23/2026", "2026-04-23") # bad: ifelse strips the Date class and returns bare numbers ifelse(grepl("/", x), as.Date(x, format = "%m/%d/%Y"), as.Date(x, format = "%Y-%m-%d")) #> [1] 20566 20566 # good parse_date_time(x, orders = c("mdy", "ymd")) #> [1] "2026-04-23 UTC" "2026-04-23 UTC" ``` ::: **Letting characters become factors silently in old code**: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- file.path(tempdir(), "file.csv") write.csv(data.frame(site = "A", n = 3), f, row.names = FALSE) # always specify class(read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)$site) #> [1] "character" class(readr::read_csv(f, show_col_types = FALSE)$site) # readr default #> [1] "character" ``` ::: **Comparing factors by value when levels differ**: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} f1 <- factor("a", levels = c("a", "b")) f2 <- factor("a", levels = c("a", "c")) f1 == f2 # works, but levels differ #> [1] TRUE # better: convert to character for cross-table comparisons as.character(f1) == as.character(f2) #> [1] TRUE ``` ::: ## Worked example: cleaning a CRF export ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(janitor) library(lubridate) library(forcats) # A stand-in for the messy export: mixed date formats, one Excel # serial date, inconsistent treatment spellings, a rare site that # should be lumped, and blank sex entries. Twenty-four rows, so that # fct_lump_min's threshold of 10 has something to bite on. crf_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "crf_export.csv") set.seed(3) tibble( `Visit Date` = rep(c("2026-01-14", "02/19/2026", NA, "2026-03-02"), 6), `Visit Date Excel` = rep(c(NA, NA, 45405, NA), 6), Treatment = rep(c("placebo", "PBO", "low dose", "HIGH DOSE"), 6), Site = c(rep("A", 12), rep("B", 10), "Y", "Z"), Sex = rep(c("F", "M", "", "F"), 6) ) |> write_csv(crf_path, na = "") # na = "NA" keeps blank Sex as an empty string rather than NA, which # is what the fct_recode below is there to handle. raw <- read_csv(crf_path, na = "NA", show_col_types = FALSE) clean <- raw |> clean_names() |> mutate( # parse mixed-format date column visit_date = parse_date_time(visit_date, orders = c("ymd", "mdy")), # convert numeric Excel dates if any visit_date = if_else(is.na(visit_date) & !is.na(visit_date_excel), excel_numeric_to_date(visit_date_excel), visit_date), # standardize treatment text treatment = str_to_title(treatment), treatment = str_replace(treatment, "^Pbo$", "Placebo"), # convert to factor with deliberate reference treatment = factor(treatment, levels = c("Placebo", "Low Dose", "High Dose")), # collapse small categories site = fct_lump_min(site, min = 10, other_level = "Other"), # recode missing-as-unknown sex = fct_recode(factor(sex), "Unknown" = "") ) |> filter(!is.na(visit_date), !is.na(treatment)) count(clean, treatment, site, sex) #> # A tibble: 10 x 4 #> treatment site sex n #> #> 1 Placebo A F 3 #> 2 Placebo A M 3 #> 3 Placebo B F 3 #> 4 Placebo B M 3 #> 5 Low Dose A Unknown 3 #> 6 Low Dose B Unknown 2 #> 7 Low Dose Other Unknown 1 #> 8 High Dose A F 3 #> 9 High Dose B F 2 #> 10 High Dose Other F 1 ``` ::: The cleaned data have dates parsed from mixed formats, treatment standardized and explicitly factored, small sites collapsed, and missing sex coded explicitly. That is, the script documents every transformation as code, rather than leaving it to memory. ## Collaborating with an LLM on types LLMs handle these packages well. The trap, as far as we have observed, is silent type coercion. **Prompt 1: parsing dates.** Paste a sample of date strings (10 examples covering the formats present) and ask: 'parse these robustly, flagging any that fail.' *What to watch for.* `parse_date_time()` with multiple orders is the canonical answer. If the LLM produces nested `ifelse` or `case_when`, push back. *Verification.* Run on the full column. Count NAs produced; investigate any unexpected ones. **Prompt 2: regex extraction.** Describe the pattern you want and provide examples. Ask the LLM to write a regex. *What to watch for.* Test the regex on edge cases the LLM may not have considered (empty strings, unusual separators, mixed case). LLM regexes often fail at the margins. *Verification.* `str_detect` and `str_extract` on a test set; count mismatches. **Prompt 3: factor reference level.** Paste a modeling formula and ask: 'is the default reference level for `treatment` clinically sensible? If not, how should it be set?' *What to watch for.* The LLM should know that alphabetical reference is rarely what you want. Specifying via `factor(..., levels = ...)` or `fct_relevel` is the canonical fix. *Verification.* Re-fit the model with the explicit reference; check coefficients match the intended interpretation. ## Principle in use Three habits keep text, categories, and dates from becoming entries on the project's bug list: 1. **Convert to factor late.** Cleaning in character; modeling in factor. Specify reference levels deliberately. 2. **Parse dates with named formats.** `parse_date_time` with explicit orders, not guesses. Watch for Excel serial numbers. 3. **Be explicit about time zones.** A datetime without a zone is a bug waiting to happen. ## Exercises 1. Using `palmerpenguins::penguins`, reorder the `species` factor by mean body mass (ascending) using `fct_reorder()`. Produce a bar plot that reflects the new order. 2. A character column contains hospital names like `'General Hospital Main Campus'`, `'Gen. Hospital'`, `'GENHOSP'`. Write a regex-based cleaning pipeline that collapses these into a single canonical level. 3. A dataset has a `visit_date` column in mixed formats. Write a pipeline that parses everything with `parse_date_time()` and flags rows that fail to parse. 4. Write a function that takes any character column and returns a tibble of value, count, and proportion. 5. Create a dataset with a datetime in PST and convert it to UTC two ways: with `with_tz` and `force_tz`. Explain the difference. **On your own data.** No answer key; the answer depends on your data. 6. Use the function from exercise 4 to audit the categorical variables in a recent analysis of yours. Report any level you did not expect. ::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true} ## Solutions to exercises 1 to 5 **1. Reorder a factor by a summary of another variable.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) penguins |> filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |> mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, body_mass_g, mean)) |> ggplot(aes(species, body_mass_g)) + stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "col") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Mean body mass by species, with the factor reordered so the bars ascend. The ordering is a property of the data, not of the alphabet.](14-types_files/figure-pdf/soln-14-1-1.pdf){fig-align='center' fig-pos='H' fig-alt='Bar chart of mean body mass for three penguin species, ascending from Chinstrap through Adelie to Gentoo.' width=100%} ::: ::: `fct_reorder()` changes the level order, and the plot follows because ggplot2 draws factors in level order. Sorting the data frame instead would not have worked. **2. Collapsing spelling variants to a canonical level.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} hosp <- c("General Hospital Main Campus", "Gen. Hospital", "GENHOSP", "Mercy Regional") canonical <- case_when( str_detect(str_to_lower(str_remove_all(hosp, "[^A-Za-z]")), "^gen") ~ "General Hospital", .default = hosp ) tibble(raw = hosp, canonical) #> # A tibble: 4 x 2 #> raw canonical #> #> 1 General Hospital Main Campus General Hospital #> 2 Gen. Hospital General Hospital #> 3 GENHOSP General Hospital #> 4 Mercy Regional Mercy Regional ``` ::: Stripping punctuation and case before matching is what lets one pattern cover all three variants. Note that this collapses `GENHOSP` correctly and leaves `Mercy Regional` alone, which is the behavior to check. **3. Parsing mixed formats and flagging failures.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} visit_raw <- c("2026-01-14", "02/19/2026", "Feb 3 2026", "not recorded") parsed <- tibble(visit_raw) |> mutate( visit_date = parse_date_time(visit_raw, orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "Bdy")), failed = is.na(visit_date) ) parsed #> # A tibble: 4 x 3 #> visit_raw visit_date failed #> #> 1 2026-01-14 2026-01-14 00:00:00 FALSE #> 2 02/19/2026 2026-02-19 00:00:00 FALSE #> 3 Feb 3 2026 2026-02-03 00:00:00 FALSE #> 4 not recorded NA TRUE ``` ::: The fourth value cannot parse, and the point of the `failed` column is that it is now data rather than a warning nobody reads. Filtering silently on `!is.na(visit_date)` would lose the count. **4. A reusable level audit.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} audit_levels <- function(df, col) { df |> count({{ col }}, sort = TRUE) |> mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) } audit_levels(penguins, island) #> # A tibble: 3 x 3 #> island n proportion #> #> 1 Biscoe 168 0.488 #> 2 Dream 124 0.360 #> 3 Torgersen 52 0.151 ``` ::: **5. `with_tz` against `force_tz`.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} t <- ymd_hms("2026-04-23 14:30:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles") with_tz(t, "UTC") # same instant, clock reads differently #> [1] "2026-04-23 21:30:00 UTC" force_tz(t, "UTC") # same clock reading, different instant #> [1] "2026-04-23 14:30:00 UTC" ``` ::: `with_tz` preserves the moment and relabels it; `force_tz` preserves the digits and moves the moment. Use `with_tz` when combining data recorded in different zones, and `force_tz` only to repair a timestamp that was stamped with the wrong zone to begin with. ::: ## Further reading - [@wickham2023r4ds] Chapters 14--18, `forcats`, `stringr`, `lubridate`. - [@bryan2019stat545] Chapters 10--13, detailed type-specific coverage. - [@grolemund2011dates], the `lubridate` paper, for the date and time-zone handling in this chapter. - The `regular-expressions.info` website, comprehensive regex reference. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-14} 1. Before R 4.0, `read.csv()` and `data.frame()` converted character columns to factors by default. This caused surprise when levels were invented, ordered, or appeared where a character string was expected, for example as merge keys. Downstream analysts had to remember `stringsAsFactors = FALSE` or suffer silent coercion. R 4.0 made `FALSE` the default, and the old default is remembered now only when reading elderly code. 2. `str_detect(string, pattern)` returns a logical vector of the same length as `string`: `TRUE` where the pattern matched, `FALSE` elsewhere. `str_extract()` returns a character vector, namely the first matching substring per input, or `NA_character_` where there was no match. In short, `str_detect` is for filtering and `str_extract` is for pulling out parts. 3. `parse_date_time(x, orders = c('ymd', 'mdy', 'Bdy'))` (or `readr::parse_date` with multiple format strings) is the tool. `lubridate::parse_date_time()` tries each order against each input and returns the first that parses. Inputs that match no format produce `NA`, which lets you flag and inspect them.
